transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-17 10:00 PST
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Eric Gomez (Redwood SE), Maya Rivera (AstraHealth Head of ML), Tom Wu (AstraHealth Infra), Priya Singh (AstraHealth CTO)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — run through the benchmark slides, hit the p50/p95 numbers vs your baseline, call out any discrepancies, and agree next steps.
[00:22] Maya: Yep that works. we looked at the summary you sent but want to talk through the tail latencies and also throughput under concurrency.
[00:35] Eric: Cool. I'll start with high level numbers. so this run was on model v2-7b-ql8 with prefix KV cache enabled and batching target 32. Redwood p50 was about 120ms, p95 ~310ms, throughput ~350 req/s at 32 concurrent workers. Baseline provider numbers from your side were p50 180ms, p95 480ms, throughput ~280 req/s.
[01:10] Tom: where were you running the Redwood tests — A100s? H100?
[01:18] Eric: Good question. For parity we ran both on A100 80GB instances — baseline provider reported similar instance types but older driver stack; we saw a slight advantage at kernel level due to our kernel selection and fused attention ops.
[01:35] Priya: The numbers look good but what about longer context lengths — our use case is often 4k token sequences. p95 could blow up there.
[01:48] Eric: We have those numbers in the spreadsheet. baseline for 4k seq we saw p95 ~1.1s on their baseline vs Redwood ~820ms with KV streaming and chunked attention. we did enable quantized path (ql8) which helped throughput.
[02:10] Maya: Any caveats? e.g., cold start behaviors?
[02:18] Jordan: yes — cold starts are higher. we saw cold-start p95 up to 2.4s depending on the model variant, but warm runs stabilize quickly with our prefix caching. we noted that in the notes.
[02:35] Tom: Are the benchmark inputs identical? sometimes tokenization differences skew p50 numbers.
[02:43] Eric: We used your sample corpus and the same tokenizer. difference mostly comes from batching efficiency and the runtime kernel optimizations. there's a note that the baseline provider's batching policy used smaller micro-batches so their throughput suffered.
[03:05] Maya: On cost, your compute is lower because throughput is higher, but how do we evaluate unit cost across bursty traffic?
[03:14] Jordan: Good point. we modeled unit cost per 1M tokens and included reserved capacity scenarios. at steady throughput Redwood's per-token cost was ~18% lower in our estimation due to batching, KV cache hit rates, and quantization. for bursty traffic, Dedicated capacity with burst pools is recommended to avoid spinning up new instances which can increase cost.
[03:42] Priya: Security checklist — SOC 2, KMS integration, SSO, audit logs, VPC peering — we need to see docs.
[03:52] Jordan: We'll send the SOC2 attestation and KMS integration guide; Eric will attach the VPC/Network runbook.
[04:05] Eric: For the POC we did a VPC-isolated test — we have audit logs enabled and can show request-level tracing. we'll include a sample trace in the spreadsheet.
[04:18] Tom: About model variants: can you fall back to a cheaper quantized variant automatically on overload?
[04:25] Eric: Yes, we can configure smart routing policies to fallback to a quantized variant or smaller model when latency SLOs are threatened. we demoed a policy in the playbook.
[04:40] Maya: There was one run where your p95 spiked to 580ms even with cache enabled — what caused that?
[04:47] Eric: Looking at logs, that was a garbage-collection-ish kernel recompile on the node after a config change, and also coincided with a burst of long-seq requests. we'll mark that as flaky and run a dedicated stress run to reproduce.
[05:05] Jordan: ok let's walk through the sheet quickly — I'll call out the rows.
[05:12] Eric: Row 12 is the main baseline comparison: identical prompt set, batch size 32 for us, 16 for baseline. Row 13 shows cold-start p95s. Row 14 shows long-seq (4k) numbers. Row 18 is throughput under concurrency 64.
[06:00] Priya: On SLA/uptime — what SLA do you provide for Dedicated?
[06:08] Jordan: Our Dedicated offering has a 99.9% uptime SLA with prioritized capacity and on-call support. we'll share the SLA doc separately.
[06:18] Maya: For our security team, how is key management handled if we want KMS? do you support customer-managed keys?
[06:26] Jordan: Yes, customer-managed KMS/HSM integration is supported in Private/Dedicated modes. for hosted we offer envelope encryption with customer-managed keys for enterprise plans.
[06:40] Tom: On the next technical testing: we want a 10k-query run with mixed seq lengths and a warm-cache scenario to see sustained p95. can you provide the runner script?
[06:50] Eric: We'll share the runner and the exact config. recommend whitelisting our test IPs.
[07:00] Maya: One more question on logging — can we get token-level latency breakdowns?
[07:06] Eric: Yes, we can export token-level traces and per-token timing, but we'll need to redact any PII depending on your policy.
[07:16] Jordan: Ok next steps recap — we'll share the spreadsheet and raw logs, Eric will produce a follow-up plan for the long-seq stress tests, and finance will join for pricing.
[07:26] Priya: We also need the benchmark runbook and a one-page summary for procurement.
[07:33] Jordan: noted. we'll include an executive one-pager.
[07:40] Tom: Regarding cost modelling for bursty traffic — can you give a dedicated vs hosted cost comparison for our expected 500-1k rps bursts?
[07:52] Jordan: we'll run that model and include it in the pricing packet.
[08:00] Maya: Can you send the follow-up by end of week? ideally Friday.
[08:06] Jordan: yes — target Friday EOD.
[08:10] Eric: I'll also spin up the reproducibility run and share logs.
[08:15] Maya: Great thanks.
[08:20] Jordan: quick note — a couple of small items to watch: (1) ensure driver/kernel parity if you run baseline tests on your side, (2) check quantization path for functional equivalence on critical prompts.
[08:35] Tom: we'll coordinate with infra to match the driver stack.
[08:40] Priya: thanks everyone, this was useful.
[08:45] Jordan: thanks all — we'll send the sheet and next steps.
[08:50] End meeting.

Notes: transcript contains minor transcription artifacts; speaker turns occasionally compressed. Attached references: link to benchmark spreadsheet (shared drive), link to VPC runbook (internal doc), pricing one-pager (to follow).
